claims.text: Conventional slow cooling produces a relatively coarse eutectic microstructure in EHEAs.
Increasing the cooling rate during casting or solidification reduces eutectic lamellar or interphase spacing.
Reduced eutectic lamellar spacing produces a more uniform and refined microstructure.
Refined lamellar spacing increases strength through a grain-refinement or Hall–Petch-type mechanism.
Refined lamellar spacing promotes more spatially distributed deformation.
More distributed deformation delays strain localization across the microstructure.
Delayed strain localization improves tensile ductility.
Rapidly cooled EHEA samples will have higher yield strength than slowly cooled samples.
Rapidly cooled EHEA samples will have greater tensile ductility than slowly cooled samples.
The simultaneous strength and ductility improvement holds only over cooling rates that refine the microstructure without introducing detrimental defects.
Excessively high cooling rates may generate thermal stresses or defects that negate the mechanical-property improvements.
The general strengthening effect of microstructural refinement is well established.
The simultaneous ductility improvement and the quantitative strength–ductility balance in rapidly cooled EHEAs remain uncertain.
Slow-cooled and rapidly cooled samples should be prepared with other processing parameters held constant.

The hypothesis is falsified if rapidly cooled samples fail to show statistically significant increases in both yield strength and ductility relative to the slow-cooled control, or if microstructural refinement is absent.
